lines.text: אתנ 105 ב
ב
אֶתְנַן Ez. 16, 34. 41, and אֶתְנָן m. (for
תְּנָן, Aleph. prosthet. from r. תָּנָה,) c.
suff. אֶתְנַנִּי.
1. a gift, hire, e. g. of a harlot, absol.
Ez. 16, 31. 34; and with זוֹנָה added
Deut. 23, 19. Metaph. of fruits and pro-
duce of the fields, regarded by idolaters
as gifts from the idols, Hos. 9, 1. Mic. 1,
2. Ethnan, pr. n. m. 1 Chr. 4, 7.
* אֲתַר Chald. subst. m. c. suff. אַתְרֵהּ.
1. a place, Dan. 2, 35. Ezra 5, 15. 6, 5.
7. In the Targums freq. Syr. et Samar.
ܐܰܬܪܳܐ id.—Hence אֲתַר דִּי the place where
Ezra 6, 3, i. q. where, a pleonasm very
common in Aramæan, Syr. ܐܰܬܰܪ ܕ; comp.
מְקוֹם אֲשֶׁר, in מְקוֹם.
2. Perh. track, i. q. Arab. إِثْرٌ, أَثَرٌ,
Ethiop. አሠር. Hence בָּאתַר for בְּאַתַר
Dan. 7, 6. 7, after, i. q. فِي اثر, عَلَى اثر,
pr. in the track; with aff. בָּתְרָךְ after
thee Dan. 2, 39. Syr. and Samar.
ܒܳܬܰܪ.
אֲתָרִים (places, regions) Atharim, pr.
n. of a place in the south of Palestine.
Num. 21, 1 דֶּרֶךְ הָאֲתָרִים by the way of
Atharim.
ב
Beth, בֵּית, the second letter of the
Hebrew alphabet; as a numeral denot-
ing 2. The Hebrew name is contracted
from בַּיִת, house, tent, to which the ear-
liest form of this letter seems to have
borne a resemblance. See Heb. Gr. p.
291. edit. 13. Monumm. Phœn. p. 21.
It passes over into the other labials,
e. g. a) Into פ, as בָּזַר and פָּזַר to dis-
perse; בָּקַע and فَقَعَ to cleave; בַּרְזֶל
Aram. פַּרְזֶל, ܦܰܪܙܠܳܐ, iron; פָּגַר and فَتَرَ
to be weak. b) Rarely into ו, as רַבְרַב,
ܪܘܪܒ, great; also into ו quiescent, as
בַּת־שׁוּעַ for בַּת־שֶׁבַע; comp. in the occi-
dental languages βόσκω vescor, pascor;
βάδω vado. c) Into מ, the sounds of
these two letters being very nearly re-
lated in the mouth of an oriental; e. g.
בְּרִיא and מְרִיא fat; מְרֹאדַךְ and בְּרֹאדַךְ
pr. n. of a Babylonish idol; محن בָּחַן to
try; זְמָן زَمَن time; זָמַר زبر to prune a
vine; דִּיבוֹן and דִּימוֹן pr. n. of a stream;
מִכְתָּם i. q. מִכְתָּב a writing, poem; Arab.
بكَّة for مكَّة Mecca. Comp. βλίττω for
μελίττω from μέλι mel, honey; scamnum,
scabellum; marmor, Fr. marbre, Engl.
marble, etc.
בְּ, before monosyllables sometimes בָּ
(see Heb. Gr. § 100), c. suff. בִּי; בְּךָ,
rarely בְּכָה Ps. 141, 8, in Pause and fem.
בָּךְ; בּוֹ, בָּהּ; בָּנוּ; בָּכֶם, בָּכֶן; בָּהֶם, בָּם,
f. בְּהֵן; Arab. بِ, rarely بَ; Ethiop.
በ; rarely ብ; Syr. ܒ; a prefix Prepo-
sition, for the origin of which see the
note at the end of the article; primarily
denoting the being and remaining in a
place, Gr. ἐν, Lat. in; then transferred
to the ideas of nearness and society or
accompaniment, at, by, with; and coupled
also with verbs of motion.
A) Pr. in, Lat. in c. abl. Gr. ἐν.—Spec.
1. in, pr. of the being in a place,
(which might be more fully and pre-
cisely expressed by בְּתוֹךְ, בְּקֶרֶב,) as
בָּעִיר in the city, בַּבַּיִת in the house, בַּבּוֹר
in the pit, בָּאָרֶץ in the land or province,
בַּאֲשֶׁר in (the place) which, i. q. where.—
Here belong also the following: a)
The formulas בְּעֵינֵי in the eyes (pr. in
the sight of the eyes), בְּאָזְנֵי, בִּפְנֵי;
comp. ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖς Hom. Il. 2. 587, in
oculis Q. Curt. 9. 4. b) The idiom
שָׁתָה בְּ ‘ to drink in a cup,’ as in Engl. i. e.
to drink what is in a cup, for ‘ to drink out
of a cup,’ Gen. 44, 5. Am. 6, 6, comp.
Chald. Dan. 5, 2. So Gr. ἐν χρυσῷ, ἐν
ποτηρίοις πίνειν Xen. Anab. 6. 1. 4. Fr.
‘boire dans une tasse,’ ‘puiser dans une
fontaine.’ The analogy of these other
languages speaks decidedly against the
explanation of Fāsi, that the vessel is
here to be conceived of as an instru
ment, q. d. to drink with a cup.

line_status.note: Header line prints three items left to right: catchword אתנ, page number 105, and catchword ב (no vowel points). Reading A drops the page number and the ב.

The Syriac word has four letters: olaph at both ends with taw and resh between (ܐܬܪܐ, i.e. atrā), as Reading A gives; Reading B drops the final olaph and misplaces the vowels. Syriac vowel points are printed (a point above the first olaph, a point under the taw, the resh dot, and a mark by the final olaph); the Hebrew אֲתַר דִּי and the English match in both readings.
Under the mem of both מְקוֹם the print shows two vertically stacked dots (shewa), not a qamets; the construct form מְקוֹם אֲשֶׁר is also what the context (Ezra 6:3 'the place where') requires.

Print shows إِثْرٌ (hamza below, kasra, sukūn, tanwīn ḍamma) first, then أَثَرٌ (hamza above, fatḥa, fatḥa, tanwīn ḍamma); A reverses the order, drops the tanwīn and wrongly puts sukūn on the second word.

The first Hebrew form shows a T-shaped qamets under the dageshed bet and no vowel under the quiescent aleph (contracted form), not patah + hataf-patah as in B; the Ethiopic and the second form are identical in both readings.

Printed left-to-right order is في اثر first (immediately after "i. q."), then a comma, then على اثر, then the line-final comma — Reading B's order, not A's. But اثر is printed bare both times (ث has only its three dots; no sukun or kasra visible), so B's اثْرِ is over-pointed. Fatha on ع/ل of على and kasra on ف are visible.

The decisive point is the middle letter of the Arabic word: the print shows a short tooth (ت) with fatha above, not the looped ج of فجر; and the gloss on the next line, "to be weak", matches فَتَرَ (to be languid), not فجر. The Hebrew and Syriac items are identical in both readings and match the print.

Under the first resh the print shows a horizontal stroke (patach), not a single dot (hireq); so רַבְרַב as in A, matching the Aramaic reduplicated form of רַב. The rest of the line (shva under first bet, patach under second resh, trailing comma) is identical in both readings.
The word is Syriac (ܪܘܪܒ, with only the inherent rish dots, no separate vowel points) as in B, but the Hebrew letter after "into" is a tall vav ו (as in A), not a yod; so each reading has one error.

After "fat ;" the first word is printed with initial מְ (plain mem, sheva) and the word at the far right of the line begins with בְּ (bet with dagesh); so the order is מְרֹאדַךְ and בְּרֹאדַךְ, as in Reading B. Reading A swaps them. All vowel points otherwise match both readings.

In both pairs the Hebrew word is printed to the left of (before) the Arabic, as in Reading B, not Arabic-first as in A. The first Arabic زَمَن does carry visible fathas; the second (زبر) shows no vowel marks in print.

On both Arabic words the only vocalisation printed is a shadda with a fatha riding above it on the kāf; there is no fatha over the initial bāʾ or mīm as Reading A gives. Reading B's Arabic matches the print; its triple space after "Mecca." is just the wide justification gap, rendered here as a single space.

Under the dageshed bet the print shows two vertically stacked dots (shewa), not a qamets stroke; also the semicolons are set tight against the Hebrew and Arabic (no preceding space), matching Reading B.
The second Ethiopic glyph has its mark at the upper-left (ብ, sixth order), not at the lower-right as ቢ would; Syriac beth is printed bare with no points.

Under the bet of the first word the print shows a qamets (horizontal bar with a descending stroke), not a shewa; so בָּעִיר (A), not בְּעִיר (B). Rest of the line is identical in both readings and matches the print.

The vowels under bet and aleph are both qamets (T-shaped, with a vertical tick below the horizontal), not sheva and segol; the bet also carries a dagesh. This is the form with the article (בָּאָרֶץ), matching Reading A.

The only difference is spacing: the opening single quotes sit directly against "boire" and "puiser" with no word space (only normal letter-fitting), so Reading B's ‘boire / ‘puiser is correct; Reading A's inserted spaces are not printed. Everything else (italic "dans" ×2, "tasse,’" with comma inside the closing quote) matches both readings.
The mark over the a in Fāsi is a flat horizontal stroke (macron), not a pointed circumflex; the i's dot is faint/worn but the letter is i.
